#### 7. congenital smooth muscle hamartoma, with or without hemihypertrophy  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.200)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-5696394)

**Proposed mechanism:** XPC (HGNC:12704) —DISRUPTS→ Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) (GO:0006289); Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) (GO:0006289) —LEADS_TO→ Xeroderma pigmentosum (HP:0000958); ACTB (HGNC:2) —DISRUPTS→ Actin cytoskeleton organization (GO:0030036); Actin cytoskeleton organization (GO:0030036) —LEADS_TO→ Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma (HP:0030978); Actin cytoskeleton organization (GO:0030036) —LEADS_TO→ Hemihypertrophy (HP:0009045). While XPC is the primary gene for xeroderma pigmentosum group C, loss-of-function mutations in ACTB, which is crucial for cytoskeletal organization, can also manifest as xeroderma pigmentosum. Simultaneously, disruptions in ACTB's actin cytoskeleton organization are implicated in the development of congenital smooth muscle hamartoma and hemihypertrophy. Thus, ACTB serves as a convergence point for these distinct disease modules through its role in cellular structure and repair.

**How to falsify it:** If mutations in ACTB are found to be exclusively gain-of-function or if pathogenic variants in ACTB are not associated with xeroderma pigmentosum phenotypes in large population databases (e.g., gnomAD with allele frequency > 0.1%) and clinical reports, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: rs12149563)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of ACTB in DNA repair and cellular structure could reveal novel therapeutic targets for both XP and hamartoma syndromes. Modulating actin dynamics might offer a unified approach to managing these diverse conditions.
